title: Nvidia in talks to put $2.5B into Mira Murati's Thinking Machines at a $40B valuation
subtitle: Accel is expected to lead a $1B tranche and Nvidia to write roughly half of a wider $5–6B round — a fourfold markup for the 18-month-old lab, whose annualized revenue is reported above $100M.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Information reported this week that Nvidia is in advanced talks to invest roughly $2.5 billion into Thinking Machines Lab, the AI startup Mira Murati founded after leaving OpenAI in early 2025. The round, expected to total between $5 billion and $6 billion, would value the company at at least $40 billion pre-money and is being lined up with Accel as lead on a $1 billion tranche. The valuation is a fourfold markup from the $10 billion pre-money at the company's July 2025 seed, when it raised $2 billion. Thinking Machines is reported to be generating annualized revenue in excess of $100 million, largely from selling businesses tools to customize AI models on their own data, while its open-weight models are free.

Two things about this deal are worth reading closely. First, the check size and structure — Nvidia writing roughly half of a growth round in a model lab — extends a pattern Nvidia has been building all year, effectively becoming a capital allocator inside the model layer rather than just a supplier of chips to it. Its March partnership with Thinking Machines already included a plan to supply at least one gigawatt of next-generation compute. Second, the markup — 4x in fourteen months, against a company that is still shipping its first commercial products — is not being driven by traditional revenue multiples. It is a bet on Murati's team and on the availability of enough compute to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic.

The wider context is that private-market AI valuations have decoupled from the ordinary rules. Anthropic overtook OpenAI in annualized revenue and private-market value earlier this year and is reportedly preparing an IPO. Cognition Labs was valued at $47 billion this week. Thinking Machines at $40 billion joins a small cluster of AI labs — most of them 18 months old — commanding pricing that would be unusual for public software companies with a decade of history. The tension for LPs and public-market investors is whether the compute pipeline these valuations imply actually gets built.

For a learner, the useful mental model here is that at the frontier of AI, valuation isn't priced on revenue — it's priced on a compound bet: (talent × compute access × time-to-next-model). Understanding why a company like Thinking Machines is worth $40 billion after eighteen months means understanding why Nvidia writing a $2.5 billion check and a gigawatt of compute is the actual product being sold to the round's other participants. That framing generalizes: whenever you see a valuation that looks impossible, ask what non-financial resource is being packaged with the equity.
